title: TLS/SSL — Securing Communication
description: Deep dive into TLS handshakes, cipher suites, certificate chains, and the performance implications of encryption in production systems.

segments.text: Every HTTPS request you make starts with a TLS handshake. It's the most important security protocol on the internet, and understanding its internals matters because misconfiguration causes both security breaches and performance disasters.

In TLS 1.2, the handshake takes two round trips. Client sends supported cipher suites. Server picks one and sends its certificate. Client verifies the certificate chain up to a trusted root CA. Then they exchange keys using RSA or Diffie-Hellman. Two full round trips before any data flows.

TLS 1.3 changed everything. It reduced the handshake to one round trip by combining key exchange and cipher negotiation into a single message. It also removed vulnerable cipher suites entirely: no more RSA key exchange, no more CBC mode, no more SHA-1. Fewer choices means fewer ways to mess up.

TLS 1.3 also supports zero-RTT resumption. If a client has connected before, it can send encrypted data in the very first packet using a pre-shared key from the previous session. Zero round trips. But there's a catch: 0-RTT data is vulnerable to replay attacks. An attacker can resend the same encrypted request.
segments.thought_prompt: If 0-RTT is vulnerable to replay, which types of requests should NEVER use it? Think about idempotency.

segments.text: RSA key exchange is dead for a reason. The client encrypts a secret with the server's public key. If the private key is ever compromised, all past traffic can be decrypted. ECDHE provides forward secrecy: each session generates ephemeral keys. Even if the server key leaks, past sessions remain safe. This is why TLS 1.3 mandates ECDHE.

Certificate verification walks a chain: your server cert, signed by an intermediate CA, signed by a root CA. Browsers ship with about 150 trusted root certificates. A common production mistake is not sending intermediate certificates, causing failures on some clients. Another: letting certificates expire. In 2020, an expired intermediate caused a Cloudflare outage.

How do you check if a certificate has been revoked? CRLs are too large. OCSP asks the CA in real time, but that's a privacy leak and a latency hit. OCSP stapling solves this: the server periodically fetches its own OCSP response and staples it to the handshake. No extra round trip, no privacy leak.

TLS adds roughly one to two milliseconds per new connection on modern hardware. With session resumption, subsequent connections drop to under 0.5 milliseconds. AES-GCM encryption on hardware with AES-NI instructions adds negligible overhead, roughly 0.3 nanoseconds per byte. The days of TLS being slow are over.

In service-to-service communication, mutual TLS verifies both sides. The server also requests and verifies the client's certificate. This is how Istio and Linkerd secure the service mesh. Every microservice gets a certificate automatically rotated by the control plane. Zero-trust networking at the infrastructure level.

Here's a production war story. A team deployed a new service with TLS 1.3 only. Everything worked in testing. In production, a legacy load balancer didn't support TLS 1.3 and silently downgraded to TLS 1.2, which the service rejected. Result: 100 percent error rate during peak traffic.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you safely roll out TLS 1.3 in a production environment with mixed infrastructure?

segments.text: Production TLS checklist: use TLS 1.3 with TLS 1.2 fallback. Enable OCSP stapling. Use ECDSA certificates over RSA — they're smaller and faster. Set HSTS headers to prevent downgrade attacks. Automate certificate rotation with Let's Encrypt or your internal PKI. Monitor certificate expiry with alerts at 30, 14, and 7 days.

TLS is non-negotiable in production. The performance cost is minimal with modern hardware. The real cost is misconfiguration: expired certs, missing intermediates, wrong cipher suites. Treat your TLS configuration as code, test it in CI, and monitor it in production.
